newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM Simitis starts work to form new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM Simitis starts work to form new cabinet.

text.p: Greek socialist Premier Costas Simitis, who won a fresh four-year mandate in elections, begins putting together his new cabinet on Monday and officials said major ministries could change hands.

"Simitis took a big risk and won. The election win is wide and gives him a free hand for sweeping changes. We will see this in his new cabinet (expected to be announced) on Tuesday," a former Simitis cabinet member told Reuters.
The defence, foreign affairs and finance ministries were up for grabs while a number of younger socialist deputies would be moved up to junior posts, officials said.
Simitis had a strong win over the opposition conservatives, with around 41.7 percent of the vote in Sunday's election which will give him about 163 deputies in the 300-seat parliament.
Socialists went wild in the streets of Athens, throwing an all-night party with horns sounding, fireworks exploding and revellers dancing in the streets.

Newspapers said Education Minister George Papandreou, the son of late socialist party founder Andreas Papandreou, or Industry Minister Vasso Papandreou (no relation) could replace Theodoros Pangalos at the foreign ministry.
Pangalos has angered Greece's allies with rude comments and has failed to win strong support within the EU for Greece in its disputes with neigbouring Turkey.

Interior Minister Akis Tshatzopoulos might head the defence ministry, replacing Gerassimos Arsenis and Finance Minister Alexandros Papadopoulos, the architect of strict tax reforms, could be moved to public works to handle millions in EU funds.
"These are changes that only Andreas Papandreou could do without being questioned. But Simitis has proven a worthy heir and his election win ended all intra-party rivalries," the official said.
"He is in full command and he will form a cabinet without compromises," he added.

Sunday's election triumph was the third straight success in Simitis's meteoric rise. He won a PASOK parliamentary vote in January to succeed Papandreou as premier, and moved on to become PASOK president at a party congress in June.
Another plus for Simitis is the absence now of a strong opposition.
Conservative New Democracy party leader Miltiades Evert resigned after the humiliating election defeat and his replacement will have the hard task of keeping the party united.
Simitis, 60, is a far cry from Papandreou whose populist welfare policies and flirting with leaders of developing countries made him a local hero but enraged EU partners and alienated Greece.
He told Greeks their future lies firmly inside the European Union and that they must make sacrifices to catch up with the rest of the group.

The newspapers said National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou, a Cambridge-educated economist, who managed to slash inflation from double digits last year to 8.5 percent in August, was expected to retain his portfolio.

He will continue his work for Greece's participation in the European Monetary Union sometime after 1999. His immediate plans include spending cuts of $1.2 billion next year to trim the public debt and curbs on public hiring.
